text: Chapter two is where data types start to genuinely diverge. We're starting with strings: varchar, nvarchar, text, and clob, and how each platform's string type menu compares to what you already know in SQL Server.

Your baseline: varchar stores non-Unicode character data, and nvarchar stores Unicode data at two bytes per character. Keep that Unicode versus non-Unicode split in mind -- it's the lens for everything that follows.

Oracle has a genuine quirk here. Plain varchar exists, but Oracle's own documentation reserves it for future behavior changes and tells you not to use it. Varchar2 is the real, recommended type. For large text beyond that, Oracle has clob, character large object.
MySQL has varchar directly, no quirk involved, plus a whole family of text types sized for different maximums: tinytext, text, mediumtext, and longtext.

PostgreSQL has both varchar and text, but here's the twist: Postgres's text type has no practical length limit, and famously, there's little to no performance difference between varchar and text. Many Postgres developers just default to text everywhere.
Next lesson, we move to numbers -- where Oracle's single, flexible NUMBER type is going to surprise you if you're used to separate integer and decimal types. See you there.
